glosses: Something of value given in return for an act.

examples.text: For catching the thief, you'll get a nice reward.

glosses: A prize promised for a certain deed or catch

examples.text: The rewards for bringing in badly wanted criminals are printed on 'dead or alive' posters.

glosses: The result of an action, whether good or bad.

examples.text: Is this the reward I get for telling the truth: to be put in jail?

Christian Benteke's first-half goal was just reward for Villa's undoubted superiority but Bradford managed to survive without further damage until half-time, before scoring the goal that takes them to Wembley for the first time since 1996.

glosses: To give a reward to or for.

examples.text: Why are you rewarding the child for misbehaving?
Why are you rewarding that bad behaviour?

glosses: To be a recompense for.

examples.text: Decorations are meant to reward the most meritous acts and services.

The Italian opted for Bolton's Cahill alongside captain John Terry - and his decision was rewarded with a goal after only 13 minutes. Bulgaria gave a hint of defensive frailties to come when they failed to clear Young's corner, and when Gareth Barry found Cahill in the box he applied the finish past Nikolay Mihaylov.

glosses: To give (something) as a reward.

examples.text:
Thenne syr Marhaus departed and within two dayes his damoysel brought hym where as was a grete tornement that the lady de Vawse has cryed
[…]
 And there syr Marhaus dyd so nobly that he was renomed
 & had somtyme doune fourty knyghtes
 and soo the serklet of gold was rewarded hym

glosses: To constitute, to compose.
To constitute, to compose.
To constitute the components of a whole.

examples.text: The words "dream interpretation" […] remind one of all sorts of childish, superstitious notions, which make up the thread and woof of dream books, read by none but the ignorant and the primitive.

glosses: To compensate, to fill in, to catch up.
To compensate for (a deficiency, defect, etc.); to supply (something missing).

examples.text: He can make up the time next week.
The Argentine found Dzeko and his killer ball was timed brilliantly for the Ivorian, who made up 90 yards, to slot in.

glosses: To compensate, to fill in, to catch up.
To compensate (for).

examples.text: What I lack in patience, I make up for in drive.
I plan to make up for my failed midterm.
Cuba took limited free market-oriented measures to alleviate severe shortages of food, consumer goods, and services to make up for the ending of Soviet subsidies.
The corn ration was drastically reduced, and it was announced that an extra potato ration would be issued to make up for it.

Meanwhile Nanny Broome was recovering from her initial panic and seemed anxious to make up for any kudos she might have lost, by exerting her personality to the utmost. She took the policeman's helmet and placed it on a chair, and unfolded his tunic to shake it and fold it up again for him.

Roger Johnson came closest to scoring for the visitors in the first half when he headed over from six yards following Lee Bowyer's cross, but he made up for that by producing some sterling defending to head clear Obinna's bullet centre.

glosses: To invent, to imagine, to concoct
To invent, to imagine, to concoct
To invent or fabricate (a story, claim, etc.).

examples.text: He was a great storyteller and could make up a story on the spot.

glosses: To assemble, to prepare.
To compile or draw up (a list, document, etc.).
To assemble, to prepare.
To put together (a substance, material, garment, medicine, etc.) into a specific form; to assemble.

examples.text: I can make up a batch of stew in a few minutes, but it will take a few hours to cook.
Like their mentors, they sang "Why Do Fools Fall In Love" and "I'm Not A Teenage Delinquent," and even had letter sweaters made up with huge "S"'s on them.

glosses: To assemble, to prepare.
To prepare (someone) for a theatrical performance by means of costume, cosmetics, etc.
To apply cosmetics.
To apply cosmetics.
To apply cosmetics or makeup to (a face, facial feature).

examples.text: Let's leave as soon as I make up my face.
She rushed into her bedroom to make up.

glosses: To make peace, to settle a dispute.
To make peace, to settle a dispute.
To resolve or settle an argument, dispute, conflict, or fight (e.g., with someone).

examples.text: They fight a lot, but they always manage to make up.
Miss Palmer and I made up, though she scolded most violently about my long absence, and attacked me about the Book without mercy.
Why somebody, why people break up / Turn around and make up, I just can't see / You'd never do that to me, would you baby?

glosses: To arrange, to advance.
To arrange (a marriage); to organise (a treaty).
To arrange, to advance.

examples.text: They in their turns made up to her, and expressed their surprize and concern at finding her in the assembly unprovided, after she had declined their invitation […].

glosses: To arrange, to advance.
To make social or romantic advances to; to pay court to.

examples.text: She thought he was making up to her—of course, at the time I believed her and I let him go, but I know now it was all nonsense.

glosses: To build, to complete.
To build, construct (a tower, city, etc.).
To build, to complete.
To build up (a bank, wall, etc.) where it has fallen away; to repair.

examples.text: Yee haue not gone vp into the gaps, neither made vp the hedge for the house of Israel.

glosses: Alternative form of makeup.
To repay (a debt owed); specifically, to recompense or reward someone for (a favour, a service rendered, etc.)

examples.text: But remember / (For that's my buſineſſe to you) that you three / From Millaine did ſupplant good Proſpero, / Expos'd vnto the Sea (vvhich hath requit it) / Him, and his innocent childe: for vvhich foule deed, / The Povvres, delaying (not forgetting) haue / Incens'd the Seas, and Shores; yea, all the Creatures / Againſt your peace: […]

He that requiteth a good turne, muſt imploy ſomevvhat of his ovvne, as he doth vvho repayeth the monie he ovveth: but he layeth out nothing vvho ſatisfieth himſelfe, no more then he giueth, vvho giueth to himſelfe. […] He therefore that requiteth a good turne pleaſureth him againe, from vvhom hee hath receiued any thing.
[T]hey requited Chriſts paſſion, and died for him vvho ſuffered for them.

"It is one of the pleasant if quite onerous duties of a man of my position to requite the services he receives—usually on a disproportionately extravagant scale."

glosses: To repay (someone) a debt owed; specifically, to recompense or reward (someone) for a favour, a service rendered, etc.

examples.text: Sir I am ſo poore to requite you, you muſt looke for nothing but thankes of me, […]

glosses: To respond to or reciprocate (feelings, especially affection or love which has been shown).

examples.text: My loue is requyted ſo louyngly / That in euery thyng that may delyght my mynde, / My wyt can not wyſhe it ſo well as I fynde

glosses: To do or give a thing in return for (something).
To retaliate or seek revenge for (an insult, a wrong, etc.).; to avenge.

examples.text: Let me this craue, ſith firſt I vvas defyde, / That firſt I may that vvrong to him requite: / And if I hap to fayle, you ſhall recure my right.

glosses: To greet (someone) in return.

examples.text: […] Chriſt and his holy apoſtles, exhort euery man to pacience and ſufferance, without requiting of an euil dede or making anye defence but vſing further ſufferance, & doyng alſo good for euill, […]

glosses: Chiefly in the form in requite for or of: synonym of requital (“compensation for damage or loss; return in kind, recompense, repayment, reward”).

examples.text: It is hard work, but they will compensate you well for it.

glosses: To make up for; to do something in place of something else; to correct, satisfy; to reach an agreement such that the scales are literally or (metaphorically) balanced; to equalize or make even.

examples.text: His loud voice cannot compensate for a lack of personality.

glosses: To adjust or adapt to a change, often a harm or deprivation.

examples.text: I don't like driving that old car because it always steers a little to the left so I'm forever compensating for that when I drive it. Trust me, it gets annoying real fast.

glosses: To reward or repay (someone) for something done, given etc.

examples.text: The judge ordered the defendant to recompense the plaintiff by paying $100.

glosses: To give (something) in return; to pay back; to pay, as something earned or deserved.

examples.text: Recompense to no man evil for evil.

examples.text: The workers were generously remunerated for their time.
